Un vendredi matin, les gens font la file: On a Friday morning, people line up on the sidewalk outside Cheskie’s, the famous kosher bakery in the Mile End.
À l’intérieur règne une atmosphère très: Inside, the atmosphere is lively, with people squeezing past one another and pointing out loaves of challah, chocolate chip cookies and triangular hamentashen.
Derrière le comptoir, on trouve souvent: Behind the counter, you will often find Cheskie himself, his wife Malky or one of their five daughters, serving the steady stream of customers coming through the door in English, French, Hebrew and Yiddish.

Cheskie est une boulangerie <em>Heimishe: Cheskie is a Heimishe bakery – a Yiddish word meaning “welcoming” that indicates the establishment sells kosher products intended for Hasidic communities.
Toutefois, chaque jour, on trouve à la b: Yet every day, the bakery draws many people of diverse origins and cultures, who order slices of babka or an assortment of colourful sugar cookies coated in chocolate and sprinkles.
Cheskie Lebowitz est un homme de petite: Cheskie Lebowitz is a small man with gentle eyes that light up above his mask. It covers only part of his long beard. He is quiet but energetic, moving from one end of the bakery to the other, making sure everything runs perfectly. Since the start of the pandemic, a sign on the front door has read: “Maximum seven people.”
« De manière générale, les affaires vont: “Generally speaking, business is going well,” says Cheskie, slipping into the back kitchen past a team of three or four masked employees who are cutting, packing and stacking mountains of boxes of rugelach and cheesecake.
Cependant, il y a eu une augmentation pe: However, there has been a noticeable increase in antisemitism and police activity in the neighbourhood since COVID-19 began, he tells us. Cheskie says he was there a few months ago when police showed up at the nearby synagogue, where people had gathered to pray.
Il a tenté de dialoguer avec les agents: He tried to talk to the officers to defuse the tense situation, but to no avail. The incident was later attributed to communication problems between the provincial government, regional Public Health and the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal.
Libby, l’une des filles de Cheskie, est: Libby, one of Cheskie’s daughters, is a journalist. She is currently writing an article on COVID-19 restrictions because she believes there needs to be a broader discussion about government accountability and the communication of emergency and extralegal decrees. “People think we don’t want to follow the rules, or that we don’t care about people,” she says, commenting on the way the media have portrayed Outremont’s Hasidic communities since the start of the pandemic. “But that’s not the point,” she adds. “It’s about continuing to live. It’s our way of life.”
Comme pour toutes les communautés montré: As with all Montréal communities, the health crisis forced Hasidim to change their way of life in order to comply with the new rules. For example, when the province closed places of worship early in the pandemic, the neighbourhood made international headlines because people organized to pray together in the street.
À mesure que le gouvernement a mis en pl: As the government introduced and changed restrictions, the new decrees began to affect people in unexpected ways. For instance, a higher proportion of large Hasidic families were tied to problems early on, when distancing measures were introduced. It was reported that some were falsely accused of violating physical distancing laws. More recently, the provincial curfew has raised problems for the observance of religious traditions and rituals, including the celebration of Shabbat, which must take place after sundown.
Lorsque Québec a imposé et modifié les r: When Quebec imposed and changed restrictions on gatherings in places of worship, the confusion was even greater, since no one knew whether the number of people allowed to gather depended on the room (as in other decrees) or the entire building.
« C’est normal de poser des questions, c: “It’s normal to ask questions, it’s normal to be upset and confused,” says Libby, exasperated, as she explains how the pandemic has affected her and her family over the past year. “There’s a valid reason, because not everything is clear,” she adds.
En plus de demander davantage de clarté: In addition to calling for more clarity and transparency in COVID-19 legislation, Libby would like to see greater attention paid to the ways some restrictions infringe on rights guaranteed by the Charter, such as freedom of religion.
« Le gouvernement a dit à un certain mom: “The government said at one point that theatres were allowed to open with 200 people inside, but synagogues were only allowed to open with 10 people inside,” she says. “It’s my right to practise my religion, more than going to the theatre, no?” she asks.
« Il est extrêmement difficile de compre: “It’s extremely hard to understand what we’re supposed to do, what they expect from us,” adds Mayer Feig, spokesperson for the Quebec Council of Hasidic Jews. He says the council has been in contact with government representatives through interfaith consultations since June, and yet misunderstandings persist.
« Il y a quelques mois, pendant la deuxi: “A few months ago, during the second wave, when we were still allowed to have 25 people per room, in accordance with Public Health rules, officers would show up at a synagogue and say, ‘You’re only allowed to have one person per building.’
Puis, ils se rendaient dans un autre end: “Then they’d go to another place and say, ‘You’re allowed to have 6 people per building,’ or ‘You’re allowed to have 25 people per building,’ or even ‘You’re allowed to have 25 people per room.’ So they were going in every direction,” he recalls.
Selon M. Feig, les agents qui se présent: According to Mr. Feig, the officers who showed up at synagogues claimed to be applying Public Health recommendations, but their directives directly contradicted what the ministry was communicating to officials. “We went to the Public Health people and said we had agreements with them about what we were supposed to do, but the SPVM says otherwise. We asked them for clarifications.
Parfois, les mesures étaient clarifiées,: “Sometimes the measures were clarified but never implemented; sometimes they were never clarified,” he says.
Le service des relations avec les médias: The SPVM’s media relations department would neither confirm nor deny these allegations and declined to comment on any details of its interventions with, or communications with, Outremont’s Hasidic community.
M. Feig affirme que, aujourd’hui, compte: Mr. Feig says that today, given the drop in the infection rate in the community, he would like the restrictions affecting places of worship to be reassessed. “There is no evidence, and there is no case on record, of a COVID-19 outbreak or epidemic being attributable to a place of worship,” he says. According to Santé Montréal, 93% of active outbreaks have instead been located in <l1>workplaces, schools, care homes and security services</l1>, many of which remain open. “If it can be done safely, why not?” Mr. Feig asks about religious gatherings. “It’s a protection provided for in our Charter of Rights.”
« Il est possible de procéder en toute s: “It’s possible to proceed safely,” he continues. “A great many manufacturing businesses and schools, which are much bigger spreaders of the virus, continue to operate, which is understandable, because they’re essential. Prayer is essential for us. As essential as alcohol, flowers, cannabis and many other things that are allowed.”

Frédéric Dejean, professeur en sciences: Frédéric Dejean, a professor of religious studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM), says the concerns voiced in Outremont reflect a broader issue for all religious traditions in Quebec.
« C’est une question de communication in: “It’s a question of intercultural communication,” he says, explaining that the province’s commitment to secularism makes these matters difficult and complicated to address. “It’s hard to maintain a balance between religious freedom and the general interest,” he continues. “And people outside these communities often don’t understand why, in certain situations, people place religious laws above government edicts.”
M. Dejean, qui a récemment coécrit un ar: Mr. Dejean, who recently co-wrote an article advocating greater sensitivity in enforcing limits on religious gatherings in communities like Outremont’s, believes it is essential that people outside the communities make an effort to better understand differences in perspective and daily life if they want to improve the situation.
« Cette crise est un indicateur de la fa: “This crisis is an indicator of how we view religious groups and religious issues in Quebec these days,” he says. “Lessons have been learned from this situation, and I hope those lessons will not be forgotten in the future.”
Fanny Magini, conseillère d’arrondisseme: Fanny Magini, a borough councillor in Outremont, says her office is aware of the problems in the borough. She agrees that better communication is needed. “I think there was a lot of confusion, and unfortunately, what happened happened,” she says of the police interventions and conflicts that took place in January.
Mme Magini affirme que son cabinet ne re: Ms. Magini says her office receives no direct communication from the province about new decrees. She has no way of knowing whether, or when, the government will impose further restrictions.
Elle ajoute néanmoins que, depuis son él: She adds, however, that since her election in 2017, her team has tried to build ties with Outremont’s Hasidic communities, including by circulating City communications in English and French and promoting City events or news in community publications such as the Heimishe News Flash in order to encourage more citizens to take part in local political life.
En ce qui concerne le fait que les restr: As for the fact that COVID-19 restrictions disproportionately affect certain religious communities in the borough, Ms. Magini says the problem is one of priorities. “There’s a majority way of thinking about what’s essential. For example, the SAQ and the SQDC are considered essential. But for these communities, what’s essential is to pray,” she says.
« Est-ce que ce que la majorité pense êt: “Is what the majority thinks is essential really essential? And does the majority take the minority’s needs into account?” she asks. “It’s a philosophical question.” A philosophical question with very real consequences for those living it – to which Ms. Magini, unfortunately, offers no solution.
En revanche, en tant que présidente du C: On the other hand, as chair of the City of Montréal’s Culture and Commerce Committee, she says she is working on implementing a major new cultural plan for the borough. The plan has been the subject of consultations and public hearings for a year, and she urges all members of the community to take part.
« Il est certain que [les contributions: “It is certain that [the contributions of Hasidic communities] are something we want to see in the cultural plan that will be implemented over the next five years,” she says. She adds that interested people can contact the City by <l1>visiting the borough’s website</l1> or its <l2>Facebook page</l2>, or by subscribing to the borough’s <l3>newsletter</l3>.
Pendant ce temps, la boulangerie est plo: Meanwhile, the bakery is dark, as Cheskie and his family celebrate Passover, a holiday that requires the entire shop and kitchen to be cleaned from top to bottom, and any remaining chametz, or yeast residue, to be eliminated.
La boulangerie restera fermée jusqu’au 2: The bakery will remain closed until April 2, while the local Jewish community celebrates the holiday with Seder meals, songs, traditional foods and games.
Avec les restrictions sanitaires imposée: With the health restrictions imposed by the government, Libby says many people will be weighing the risks of spending time with their families during this important holiday.
S’il va de soi que la loi doit être resp: While the law must of course be respected, life goes on. “It’s not a life of fear,” says Libby. “It’s a life of family and community.”
